source: Abiotic Disorders, Nutritional Deficiencies & Differential Diagnosis (Section 1)
text: Section 1: The Critical Necessity of Differential Diagnosis. A critical vulnerability in clinical agriculture is the frequent misdiagnosis of abiotic (non-infectious) physiological disorders as fungal or bacterial plant diseases. Applying fungicides, bactericides, or systemic chemicals to abiotic environmental disorders wastes economic resources, contaminates ecosystems, and fails to remedy the underlying physiological stress. Section 2: Blossom End Rot (BER) of Tomato and Pepper - NOT A FUNGUS! - Clinical Presentation: Initiates as a water-soaked, light tan sunken spot directly at the blossom end (distal fruit tip opposite the stem calyx) of rapidly developing green tomatoes, peppers, and eggplants. The lesion rapidly enlarges, darkens, and flattens into a distinct, circular, dry, leathery, sunken black or dark brown plate. - The Diagnostic Pitfall: Secondary opportunistic saprophytic fungi (such as Alternaria or black molds) often colonize the dead leathery tissue, causing growers to mistakenly identify BER as 'early blight' or 'fruit rot' and spray copper or chlorothalonil. - True Physiological Cause: Blossom End Rot is caused exclusively by a localized Calcium (Ca2+) deficiency within the rapidly expanding distal fruit pericarp cells. Calcium is an immobile structural element bound in cell wall middle lamellae as calcium pectate.

source: Abiotic Disorders, Nutritional Deficiencies & Differential Diagnosis (Section 2)
text:
Calcium is an immobile structural element bound in cell wall middle lamellae as calcium pectate. Because calcium is transported exclusively through xylem transpiration flow driven by water loss from leaves, leafy canopies transpire far more water than fruit. When soil moisture fluctuates (e.g. drought stress followed by heavy deluge, or irregular watering cycles), calcium fails to reach the distal fruit tip, causing cell wall collapse and dry necrosis. - Correct Clinical Remedy: DO NOT APPLY FUNGICIDES. Maintain uniform, consistent soil moisture through automated drip irrigation; apply organic mulch (5-10 cm straw or wood chips) to prevent rapid soil drying; avoid excessive ammonium-nitrogen (NH4+) fertilizer, which directly competes with Ca2+ ions for root uptake; verify soil pH is maintained between 6.2 and 6.8. Section 3: Herbicide Drift vs. Viral Infections. Synthetic auxin growth-regulator herbicides (notably 2,4-D, dicamba, and triclopyr) applied to nearby turfgrass or grain fields easily volatilize and drift on wind currents over miles:
- Diagnostic Symptoms: Susceptible crops (especially tomatoes and grapes) exhibit dramatic downward epinasty, twisting of petioles, strap-like leaf narrowing, thickening of leaf veins, and parallel venation resembling a folded fan or duck foot.

source: Abiotic Disorders, Nutritional Deficiencies & Differential Diagnosis (Section 3)
text: - Differential Diagnosis: Often misdiagnosed as Tomato Mosaic Virus (TMV) or Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus. Differential rule: Herbicide drift symptoms appear suddenly across an entire greenhouse or field within 24-48 hours after wind/lawn spraying, with all plants of a similar age affected simultaneously; viral infections start on isolated plants and spread progressively via vectors or mechanical pruning lines over weeks. Section 4: Macro- and Micronutrient Chlorosis Differential Matrix. - Iron (Fe) Deficiency Chlorosis: Characterized by brilliant, sharp interveinal chlorosis (leaf veins remain dark green while interveinal areas turn pale yellow to white) strictly on the YOUNGEST, uppermost terminal foliage. Caused by high soil pH (>7.5) rendering iron insoluble. Corrected with chelated iron (Fe-EDDHA). - Nitrogen (N) Deficiency: General, uniform, pale yellow-green chlorosis initiating on the OLDEST, lowermost senescence foliage first, as the plant mobilizes mobile nitrogen to support young growing tips. Corrected with nitrogen fertilizer. - Magnesium (Mg) Deficiency: Interveinal chlorosis with reddish-purple margins occurring primarily on LOWER mature leaves (because Mg is mobile in phloem). Corrected with magnesium sulfate (Epsom salts). Section 5: Sunscald, Catfacing, and Physiological Edema.

Section 5: Sunscald, Catfacing, and Physiological Edema. - Sunscald: Bleached, white, papery, sunken blisters on shoulders of green fruit directly exposed to intense sunlight following sudden defoliation (e.g. after pruning or black spot leaf drop). Not infectious. - Catfacing: Severe malformation, puckering, scarring, and deep cavity bands at the blossom end of heirloom tomatoes. Caused by cold ambient temperatures (<12°C / 54°F) during flower bud differentiation, disrupting pistil carpel fusion. - Physiological Edema (Oedema): Blister-like, water-soaked, corky bumps on lower leaf surfaces and petioles. Occurs in greenhouse plants when warm, wet soil drives root water uptake while cool, humid, overcast air halts foliar transpiration, bursting leaf mesophyll cells.
